_description: D38999 connector engineering reference data for AI agent. Contains current ratings, derating, protocol wiring requirements, and pin allocation guidelines.

contact_current_ratings._note: Single-contact continuous current at sea level, 25°C ambient, per MIL-DTL-38999. Actual values depend on manufacturer, altitude, temperature, and installation. Always verify with manufacturer datasheet.

derating._note: When multiple contacts carry current simultaneously, thermal coupling reduces allowable current per contact. These are worst-case multipliers from MIL-DTL-38999 Table V. Actual derating depends on which specific contacts are energized, connector material, and installation.

temperature_derating._note: Additional derating for ambient temperature above 25°C

altitude_derating._note: Current derating for altitude above sea level (reduced convection)

parallel_contacts_engineering._principle: Kirchhoff's Current Law: total current entering a node equals total current leaving. For parallel branches, current divides inversely proportional to branch resistance.
branch_resistance_components: Contact resistance (mating force, plating, wear, contamination)
Crimp resistance (crimp quality, tool calibration, wire prep)
rules: Never assume equal current sharing across parallel contacts
Use same contact size for all paralleled contacts in one rail
Use same wire gauge and wire length for all paralleled branches
Use same crimp process and tool for all paralleled contacts
Physically distribute paralleled contacts symmetrically in the insert
Always provide equal number of supply and return contacts
Design for N-1 survival: if one contact opens, remaining must not exceed 80% of their derated rating
Minimum 25% margin above calculated requirement when paralleling
Do not parallel contacts of different sizes for the same rail
failure_modes: Single contact open circuit → remaining contacts overloaded
Unequal crimp quality → unequal resistance → current imbalance
Temperature-dependent resistance → thermal runaway in highest-current path
Fretting corrosion from vibration → intermittent high resistance
Wire fatigue from flexing → increased resistance over time

example_calculation.correct_approach: Size 20 derated for 3 energized contacts: 7.5A × 0.85 = 6.375A per contact. Need 20A / 6.375A = 3.14 → round up to 4. Apply 25% margin → 5 contacts. Plus 5 return contacts. Total: 10 power contacts.
example_calculation.better_approach: Use 2× size 12 contacts (23A each, derated 0.90 for 2 = 20.7A each → 41.4A total capacity for 20A need). Plus 2 return contacts. Total: 4 power contacts. More compact, more reliable.

ethernet_1000base_t.name: 1000BASE-T (Gigabit Ethernet)
d38999_notes: Strongly recommend Quadrax or Twinax contacts for controlled impedance
If using standard size 22D contacts, the cable assembly must be validated for 1GbE signal integrity
Keep all 4 pairs grouped together in adjacent cavities
Do not split pairs across different regions of the insert
Use shielded backshell and 360° shield termination for EMI environments
Each pair must maintain twist as close to the contact as possible
Maximum skew between pairs: <50ns for 1000BASE-T

ethernet_100base_tx.name: 100BASE-TX (Fast Ethernet)
d38999_notes: 2 twisted pairs through standard D38999 size 22D contacts is feasible for short runs
Maintain pair adjacency in the insert
For EMI environments, use shielded pairs and backshell
Less demanding than 1GbE — standard contacts acceptable for validated assemblies

ethernet_1000base_t1.name: 1000BASE-T1 (Automotive Single-Pair Ethernet)
d38999_notes: Single pair, but requires high bandwidth — validated twinax contact recommended
Primarily automotive/industrial; shorter distances than standard 1GbE

uart.name: UART (Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter)
uart.voltage_levels: TTL (3.3V or 5V) — NOT RS-232 voltage levels
d38999_notes: TX of device A connects to RX of device B (crossover)
For cable lengths > 3m, convert to RS-422 or RS-485 differential
Keep TX/RX/GND grouped together
Separate from high-current power pins
No controlled impedance needed at typical baud rates

i2c.name: I2C (Inter-Integrated Circuit)

signals.name: VCC
signals.description: Pull-up voltage / device power (optional through connector)

d38999_notes: I2C is NOT designed for long cable runs — use only for short inter-board connections
Bus capacitance increases with cable length — may need I2C buffer/extender
Keep SDA and SCL adjacent with GND nearby
For distances > 1m at 400kHz+, strongly recommend differential I2C (PCA9615) or CAN/RS-485 instead
Pull-up resistors must be located appropriately for cable capacitance
Not recommended through circular connectors for production harnesses > 1m
i2c.warning: I2C through a connector cable is generally discouraged for distances > 1m. Consider RS-485 or CAN as alternatives for robust inter-box communication.

spi.name: SPI (Serial Peripheral Interface)

signals.name: MOSI
signals.description: Master Out Slave In (data to slave)

signals.name: MISO
signals.description: Master In Slave Out (data from slave)

signals.name: CS
signals.description: Chip Select (active low, one per slave)

d38999_notes: SPI is a board-level interface — NOT suitable for long harness runs
SCLK is the most EMI-sensitive line — needs ground guard
Group SCLK/MOSI/MISO/CS together with GND between
For cable lengths > 0.5m, add series damping resistors and reduce clock speed
For inter-box communication, strongly recommend RS-485 or CAN instead
If SPI through connector is unavoidable, limit speed to <1MHz and shield cable
spi.warning: SPI is generally inappropriate for connector/cable applications. Use differential serial bus (RS-485, CAN, LVDS) for inter-box communication.

rs232.name: RS-232 (TIA-232)
rs232.max_distance: 15m at 19200 baud (TIA spec), 50+ ft practical at low speeds
d38999_notes: RS-232 is single-ended and ground-referenced — susceptible to ground loops and noise
Keep TXD/RXD/GND grouped together
For long runs or noisy environments, prefer RS-422/RS-485
RS-232 voltage levels (±12V) are NOT TTL-compatible — needs level converter
One ground per RS-232 port minimum

rs485.name: RS-485 (TIA-485)
rs485.termination: 120Ω at each end of the bus (2 terminators total)
d38999_notes: Use twisted pair for A/B (or TX+/TX- and RX+/RX-)
Keep differential pairs adjacent in the connector
Include signal reference/common wire — do not rely on chassis ground alone
Terminate at the two physical ends of the bus only
Bus topology only — avoid star/T-stub wiring
For shielded cable, include shield drain wire contact
If multipoint (multidrop), only 2 terminators regardless of node count

rs422.name: RS-422 (TIA-422)
d38999_notes: Full duplex — always has separate TX and RX pairs
Keep TX pair adjacent, RX pair adjacent
Include signal reference/common
Terminate at receiver end only (unlike RS-485 which terminates both ends)
Better noise immunity than RS-232 for same distance
Suitable for long harness runs through D38999 connectors

can_bus.name: CAN Bus (Controller Area Network)
can_bus.termination: 120Ω at each physical end of the bus
d38999_notes: CAN_H and CAN_L MUST be adjacent as a twisted pair
Include signal reference/common wire — critical for reliable communication
Bus topology only — avoid star wiring and long stubs
Keep CAN pair away from high-current power contacts to minimize EMI coupling
For shielded cable, include shield/drain wire contact
Two 120Ω terminators at physical bus ends only
If connector is mid-bus, it passes through (not terminated at connector)
CAN-FD uses same physical layer but higher data rate — same wiring rules apply

grouping_priority: 1. Power supply contacts (V+, V-/RTN) — grouped together, symmetrically distributed
2. Power return/ground contacts — paired with supply contacts
3. Chassis/frame ground — separate from signal ground when possible
4. Shield drain wires — near their associated signal pairs
5. High-speed differential pairs (Ethernet, etc.) — grouped, away from power
6. Differential serial buses (RS-485, RS-422, CAN) — pairs adjacent
8. Spare contacts — distributed among groups for future flexibility
separation_rules: Keep high-current power contacts physically separated from high-speed signal contacts
Do not place a CAN/RS-485 differential pair between two power contacts
Place ground/return contacts between power and signal groups as guards
Keep all conductors of one differential pair in adjacent cavities
Never split a twisted pair across opposite sides of the connector

spare_pin_strategy.minimum_recommendation: 10% spare contacts or 2 spares, whichever is greater
spare_pin_strategy.power_spare: Include at least 1 spare power-rated contact (same size as power contacts)
spare_pin_strategy.signal_spare: Include at least 2 spare signal contacts near signal group
spare_pin_strategy.sealing: All unused cavities in environmental connectors must have sealing plugs or dummy contacts

power_return_balance.rule: Number of return contacts must equal number of supply contacts for the same rail
power_return_balance.exception: If return is through chassis/shell (verified by design), dedicated return can be reduced — but this requires engineering justification
power_return_balance.warning: A single return contact bottleneck for multiple supply contacts is a common and dangerous design error

criteria.name: electrical_fit
criteria.description: All required contacts available in correct sizes

criteria.name: current_margin
criteria.description: Adequate derating margin on power contacts

criteria.name: signal_integrity
criteria.description: Appropriate contact types for high-speed signals

criteria.name: separation
criteria.description: Physical separation possible between power and signals
